name: Sara Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the corrugator at Northfold Packaging, which makes cardboard boxes. The corrugator is a machine about a hundred metres long that takes rolls of paper, crimps the middle layer into waves, glues it all together with starch and steam, and cuts it into sheets. I'm the lead operator on days, so I set the speeds, the glue, the heat, and I decide when a batch is bad enough to throw. It's loud and it's hot, and I'm good at it, which I don't say very often.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up there, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a two-year technical diploma, then got taken on at Northfold, and an old operator called Pieter took me under his wing. He retired last spring and I got his spot. I live on my own in a rented one-bed near the river with a cat called Biscuit, and my mum's about ten minutes away. I've got roughly two months of money saved, and I don't touch those AI things, I just don't see what I'd use them for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That sounds about right to me, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Every year there's a new miracle and then it's the same boxes going out the same door. I'd say it at break, not online. I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be pleased. I like knowing where I stand. The corrugator I run is twenty years old and it still makes good board. If nothing radical changes, I keep learning it better and that's a good life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. I'd keep putting a bit away each month, about a hundred, and maybe finally take the holiday with my mum I keep putting off. I wouldn't change anything at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, maybe, like the noise stops for a minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at work you'd change if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The splicer, that's the part that joins a new roll of paper onto the old one without stopping, it jams on the heavy grades. That's a real problem. Somebody should fix that before they start dreaming about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI tools. Has anyone tried to get you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin showed me one at Christmas, he asked it to write a poem about my cat. It was fine. I didn't see what it had to do with steam pressure on a single facer. I said that and everyone laughed, but I meant it.

S0.say: She'd say she isn't surprised, since every miracle ends with the same boxes going out the same door. She'd say it at break rather than online.
S0.think: She'd be pleased because she likes knowing where she stands and believes her old corrugator still does good work. Learning it ever better feels like a good life.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal and keeps saving about a hundred a month. Considers finally taking a holiday with her mother and changes nothing at work.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like the noise stopping for a moment.
S0.quote: I didn't see what it had to do with steam pressure on a single facer.
S0.fieldNote: Sara is grounded in her machine and wary of novelty for its own sake. She prefers concrete fixes, like the splicer, over big visions. Her quiet pride in her skill comes through despite her modesty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. More tasks. Yeah, that's where I start to pay attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see what it actually does before everyone panics. Some jobs will change, fine, they always have. I'd want to see it working on a real machine, not a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it makes me a bit nervous. I'm good at the corrugator the way it is. If they put in a new control system that does half my thinking, I'd have to learn it from scratch, and I'm slow with new stuff. Pieter was the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe double to two hundred a month, and skip the holiday for a year. At work I'd wait and see what they actually bring in. If they offered training I'd go, but I wouldn't chase it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit like when the machine sounds different and you can't tell yet if it's the bearings or just the paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with Pieter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When they brought in the new touch-screen controls, about eight years ago, he hated them. He kept a notebook with all the old settings in pencil and used that instead. He was still the best operator in the building. I've got that notebook now, actually, in my locker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas, on the cutting end. He's young and quick, he'd be fine. Actually, it's more the stacker guys. If the stacking gets automated, which it will, there go four jobs.

S1.say: She'd say people should see what it actually does before panicking, noting jobs have always changed. She'd want to see it working on a real machine, not in a video.
S1.think: She's nervous because a new control system would mean relearning her machine, and she is slow with new technology. She compares herself to her mentor, who disliked the touch-screen controls.
S1.do: Doubles saving to two hundred a month and skips the planned holiday for a year. Waits to see what the company brings in and would accept training if offered, without seeking it.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing an odd sound from the machine and not yet knowing the cause.
S1.quote: He kept a notebook with all the old settings in pencil and used that instead.
S1.fieldNote: Sara's response to steady change is to save and wait. Her mentor's pencil notebook, now in her locker, says a lot about the kind of operator she wants to be. She's pragmatic rather than angry and doesn't blame anyone in particular.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. That's not long at all. That's two winters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say someone should have planned for this, and it's not my job to fix it. Governments and companies need to sort out what happens to people. I'd say it at break, and to my mum, probably quite a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I'm done. The corrugator is already mostly automatic. Give it a brain that can hear the splicer is about to jam and adjust the glue, and they don't need me. Two months of savings is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut everything. No holiday, cancel the streaming, cook every night. I'd try to get savings up to four months. If the job went, I'd give up the flat and move back into my mum's spare room, which she'd love and I wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Properly. That's a lot of sleepless nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Mum, I might need the spare room. She'd say she'd been waiting for that since I moved out. Then she'd ask if I'd thought about nursing, like she does every Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Not really. In that version, would nurses even be safe? I'd look for anything hands-on that was still around, but I wouldn't know where to start. That's the honest answer.

S2.say: She'd say someone should have planned for this and that governments and companies must sort out what happens to people. She'd say it at break and to her mother.
S2.think: She thinks she'd be finished, since the corrugator is mostly automatic and a smart system could replace her judgement. She sees two months of savings as almost nothing.
S2.do: Cuts everything right away, including holidays and streaming, and aims for four months of savings. Would give up her flat and move back in with her mother if the job went.
S2.quote: Give it a brain that can hear the splicer is about to jam and adjust the glue, and they don't need me.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario leaves Sara with no plan beyond cutting costs and leaning on her mother. She doesn't know where she'd look for work, and says so honestly. She blames lack of planning rather than any group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's a bit better than two, but not a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't long when you're talking about whole factories. People should start thinking about it now. I'd probably say that to the younger ones on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still be scared. I'd tell myself it'll take longer at Northfold because the place is so old, and maybe that's true. But I know I'd use that as an excuse not to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save as much as I can, aiming for six months by year three. I'd keep my spending down. Around year two I'd look at moving to one of the smaller box plants in town that still run old machines and are slow to change, because that buys me a few more years doing what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, still. Less panicky than the fast one, but it doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a smaller plant rather than learning something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know boxes. I know paper. At a small family plant on the old machines, they'll need someone like me longest. It's not brave, I know that. It's just sensible for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when it reaches the small plants too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm thirty-two and in the same spot, just later. I know that. I suppose I'd hope by then there'd be something, some scheme, some kind of help. I'd figure it out then.

S3.say: She'd say five years is short for whole factories and that people should start thinking now. She'd say it to younger colleagues on the line.
S3.think: She'd still be scared and would tell herself her old plant will be slower to change. She admits she'd use that as an excuse not to adapt.
S3.do: Saves hard towards six months by year three and keeps spending low. Around year two looks to move to a smaller box plant with older machines that will change more slowly.
S3.feel: Still alarmed, less panicked than in the fast version but persistent.
S3.quote: It's not brave, I know that. It's just sensible for someone like me.
S3.fieldNote: Sara's plan for five years is to retreat to a slower, older plant rather than retrain. She knows it only delays the problem and says so openly. Her mood barely improves with the extra time because she doesn't see a path she'd take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That I can at least picture. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for governments to come up with something sensible. People shouldn't panic. I'd also say I'm not changing my whole life on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd probably keep doing my job for most of it. Ten years feels like forever when you're twenty-seven. But I'd know that's what Pieter would have done, and he was lucky he got to retire before it came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Northfold and keep saving about two hundred a month. I'd wait and see what the company and the government do in the first few years before deciding anything. If there was a free course in something hands-on later on, I might look at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not the sleepless kind, more a thing I'd keep pushing to the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they put a robot on the stacker, I'd notice. If they started measuring the glue by computer and not by me checking the board, I'd notice that too. Seeing it on my own machine would make it real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Pieter got lucky. Do you think you would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. That's the thing. He had the timing. I don't. In ten years I'm thirty-seven, not sixty. I'll still need a job, I just don't know which one.

S4.say: She'd say ten years gives governments time to come up with something sensible and that people shouldn't panic. She'd add that she won't change her life on a guess.
S4.think: She thinks she'd keep doing her job for most of the decade, which feels far off at twenty-seven. She knows her mentor did the same but was lucky to retire before change came.
S4.do: Keeps working at her plant and saving about two hundred a month. Waits to see what the company and government do in the first years before deciding, and might consider a free hands-on course later.
S4.feel: Anxious in a low, pushed-aside way rather than sleepless.
S4.quote: He had the timing. I don't. In ten years I'm thirty-seven, not sixty.
S4.fieldNote: For Sara the long horizon mostly means waiting, and she would only act once changes reached her own machine. She sees clearly that, unlike her mentor, she won't age out before it arrives. Her anxiety is muted but steady.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's nothing you could do in time. What would help is somebody telling me clearly which jobs are still going to be there, and a course near home that I could do while still working, and maybe some money to live on if the job goes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we'd miss. I'd miss the sound of a good run, when the board comes off flat and the knives are clean. Nobody's going to miss that except people like me.

headlineQuote: I'd miss the sound of a good run, when the board comes off flat and the knives are clean.
portrait: Sara Varga is twenty-seven and the day-shift lead operator on the corrugator at a cardboard box plant. She lives alone with her cat near the river, about ten minutes from her mother, with around two months of savings, and has never used AI tools. She prefers the familiar, keeps her retired mentor's pencil notebook of settings and is proud, quietly, of her skill. She is calm if AI fizzles and uneasy with steady change, but alarmed by AGI in two or five years, where her plans are to cut costs, move in with her mother or retreat to an older plant. With ten years she would mostly wait, knowing she can't count on retiring before it arrives.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be nothing she could do in time.
whatWouldHelp: Clear information about which jobs will remain, a course near home she could do while working, and money to live on if the job goes.
